speechtext:
I am rising on a question of privilege in connection with various newspaper reports containing alleged statements attributed to me. These statements are without foundation. The Ottawa Journal of August 2 published an article by Richard Jackson with a subheading in quotation marks reading as follows: "Breach Civil Service Propriety". This statement I did not make. It is without foundation. Then there follows this paragraph in quotation marks:
"There is no doubt but that unauthorized access was allowed to the department's confidential files", said Mr. Churchill, "for the quotations from the report are both very copious and quite accurate."
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is without foundation. Further down in the article I am alleged to have said that I intend to run this thing down. The words "run this thing down" are in quotation marks. That statement is without foundation. Toward the end of the article occurs the following paragraph:
Mr. Churchill made it plain that while his investigation would be "thorough"-
The word "thorough" is in quotation marks.
-it would not be actually "tough".
The word "tough" is in quotation marks. That statement, Mr. Speaker, is without foundation. The Toronto Telegram of August 2 carries an article written by Peter Demp-son. The third paragraph of that article reads as follows:
Trade minister Churchill summed up his reaction to the leak in one word "violent"-
57071-3-192J
The word "violent" is in quotation marks. That statement is without foundation. Further on I am alleged to have said:
"Well I guess they are authentic all right"-
That statement is without foundation. The Globe and Mail of Monday, August 4, carries an article by Clark Davey in which he attributes to me the following statement which he puts in quotation marks:
"There is no doubt about it", he said, "the newspaper report is based on the actual report".
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is without foundation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
That notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 15(3), the business and procedure on Monday, August 11, 1958, and on every Monday thereafter until the end of this session, shall be as for Monday (government day), and
That on Monday, August 11, 1958, and on every sitting day thereafter, until the end of this session, this house shall meet at 11 o'clock a.m., and in relation thereto that the provisions of standing order 2(1) shall be suspended.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
So far as the first part of this motion is concerned, Mr. Speaker, the official opposition will not object to it. So far as the second part of the motion is concerned, the extending of the time of sitting as from Monday, August 11, so that we will meet every morning, including Saturday morning, we do take objection.
It will be recalled that a short time ago the leader of the house introduced a resolution extending the hours of sitting, and we did not object. In fact we supported it on the ground that we were, so we thought, approaching the end of the session and perhaps some provision should be made for extending the hours of sitting. The provision that was made on that occasion did not interfere with the work of the committees, at least to any alarming extent, so we supported it.
We now have a motion before us which would make committee work very difficult, if not impossible, in the sense that the committees could hardly meet except during the hours when the house is in session. Some committees have just begun their work and others are in the middle of their work. The

Business of the House
committee on external affairs has just begun its work. It was meeting this morning, and it is now suggested that it should meet this afternoon also.
We object, therefore, to this second extension of the hours of sitting because of the effect it will have on our committee work. Perhaps by next Monday we would be in a better position to make an estimate of how the committee work is getting on and when it is likely to finish. Perhaps we would be in a better position then to relate the extension of hours to the work of the committees than we are at the moment.
We object also to this motion because it provides for parliament meeting morning, afternoon and evening, except on Wednesday and Saturday, for an indeterminate period. I suggest it certainly is indeterminate because we have no idea what legislation the government is going to introduce. So far as we know there has been no planning of the work for the remainder of the session. There is some important legislation forecast in the speech from the throne which is not yet on the order paper. We do not know in what form it will be on the order paper, and we do not know what length of time will be required to complete it. We may be here for weeks, and that is not a prospect that anyone contemplates with great pleasure, I am sure.
Until we get some indication as to the planning of the work ahead, the legislation which has to be passed this session, surely it is not right to ask the house to meet morning, afternoon and evening, with the exception of Wednesday and Saturday, especially when the committee work is continuing. This is the way we approach this particular resolution.
We have done our best on this side, by inquiries we have addressed to the leader of the house and the Prime Minister from time to time, to get some specific information on the planning of the work ahead. There have been occasions this session when at 10 o'clock at night we have asked about the work ahead and it has not been possible to tell us definitely and with assurance what would be done even the next day, let alone two or three days or a week or two ahead.
I recall-and I mentioned this point the other day when 1 was talking about this matter-how the former leader of the opposition, Mr. George Drew, used to rise in his place day after day and attack the government in vigorous terms because the government of that day, so he said, did not give the opposition sufficient advance notice of the work to come before parliament and did not plan ahead.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that on the order paper today there is no evidence of planning

ahead. Until we get some notice of what we are going to have to do and how long it may be necessary to stay here to do it, and until we get further information as to the work of the committees and when that work is likely to be completed, it is not possible for us to support that part of this resolution.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we now have before us a motion moved by the government. It can be broken down into two principles. In the first section the principle means that starting next Monday, that day until the end of the session shall be government days. In the second section the principle is one which is going to quite radically change the hours of sitting of this house.
I desire to open my remarks in this way. Within your view, Mr. Speaker, I am going to hold in my hand, as I now do, a copy of the standing orders of the House of Commons, an edition which as revised came into effect in the year 1955. That revision of the standing orders was not introduced into the house until there had been a lengthy study by a committee representative of all parties of this house; and if my memory serves me correctly, it was brought in as an almost unanimous recommendation on the changes in standing orders. I am certain that Your Honour will remember the necessary resolution which was brought into this house and the speeches that were made at that time as to the meaning of the revision. It had a recognition of the responsibilities of government and a recognition of the responsibilities and the rights of minorities.
In particular I draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that when this revision of standing orders was introduced, the protection of minorities not only referred to minority groups in this house but also referred to minority rights in this house and minority rights in a number of particulars affecting the majority of the members of this house, namely the rights of private members irrespective of whether they sit on the government side, in the official opposition or in any other group in this house. Mr. Speaker, I should just like to refresh your memory, although I do not think it is necessary, and the memories of those who were here in 1955 and who now sit on the government side as to the fundamental meaning of standing orders. Keeping that in mind, and not forgetting what was said in 1955, we now have before us a motion introduced by the government to once again during this session-I repeat once again- ask this parliament to take action notwithstanding something which is contained in the revised standing orders of 1955, which we were told was put there basically for the

protection of minority parties, and most certainly for the protection of private members.
The first part of the motion is to remove any possibility after next Monday of a private member having any right whatsoever in this house, for the balance of this session, so far as bills or resolutions are concerned. Without reference to any record whatsoever I think I could make quite a speech on that subject, but I do not intend to do so. I am going to take a leaf out of the Conservative book while that party was the official opposition in this house, and will also refer to some things which have been said since that party has formed the government.
In referring to the record, Your Honour, I am going to ask the government and, since he seems to be so interested, the leader of the house, to answer a question when I have completed my remarks. Is there a difference so far as the government is concerned in the responsibility of the government and the responsibility of the official opposition, once that opposition takes office? If the government party is the party of principle and believe in what they said for over 20 years while they were on this side of the house, why do they this afternoon completely deny every expression of principle on an issue of this nature, about which they were so vociferous for over 20 years-

-and in particular during the
past five years?
I do not often indulge in a great deal of quoting, but in respect to this motion I intend to do so; and every word I am going to quote will be taken from the official record of Hansard. You will see, Mr. Speaker, that I have the volumes in front of me and my references will be to the remarks of the former leader of the Conservative party, Hon. George Drew, the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton).

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

Mr. Speaker, hon. members should be very careful, because I have books under the desk in case any hon. member over there thinks he is being overlooked.
I desire to introduce this question of principle by means of what I believe is a most important statement, because it was made by an hon. gentleman who previously had the honour to sit in your place, Mr. Speaker, namely Mr. Speaker Fauteux. Both he and Dr. Beauchesne spoke on this subject. I wish to read a very short excerpt from the remarks of Mr. Speaker Fauteux, made with the assistance of Dr. Beauchesne, who at the time in
Business of the House
question was clerk of the house, when they presented a report to the House of Commons in 1947. This can be found in the Journals of the House of Commons for 1948. It is found on page 10, and this is what it says:
The mere object of shortening sessions must not be the aim of any revision of our rules.
In view of what the Leader of the Opposition said a few moments ago I ask that he take note of that. I continue:
The duties of a representative parliament are too important to be performed in a hurry. No question should be decided until it has been fully discussed. Yet no member of the house wants delays based on rulings or practice which may have been necessary when they were established centuries ago but which have no reason to exist at the present time. Conditions have changed. Although every effort ought to be made to economize time, every shade of opinion has the right to find expression and members who desire to give their views should not be prevented from doing so.
That statement, sir, as I pointed out is found in the Journals of the House of Commons for 1948, a submission made by Mr. Speaker Fauteux and Dr. Beauchesne. I say that this in itself negates the principle outlined in the first section of the motion now before us because this is a motion to deny from Monday next any opportunity for a private hon. member of this house, irrespective of whether he sits on the government or opposition side, to pursue any motion, resolution or bill that he now has on the order paper.
Having used that authoritative introduction, I wish now to take the minds of hon. gentlemen, who sit on the government side of the house, back just a couple of years or so and review what was said by some of them when they sat in opposition. I intend to refer them first to some remarks made by Hon. George Drew, who for many years was the leader of the Conservative party in opposition in this house. I refer hon. gentlemen to Hansard of February 3, 1954, at page 1728. Referring to the Liberal government that was then in power, Mr. Drew said on that occasion:
I hope the government will not suggest to us that private members can make no useful suggestions which they themselves have not already thought of. If they were to take that position it would surely be strangely inconsistent with the arguments which have been made in support of other measures still before this house for consideration. No; the government must, in view of the argument they have been making, support the argument that they believe that private members have an important place here and that private members have much to contribute.
I hope there are many hon. gentlemen opposite, and I think there are, who have much to contribute; because on reading the

Business of the House
order paper I find that there are many motions standing in the names of hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of the house. I continue:
They have been urging that private members have plenty of time-
May I repeat that phrase, "plenty of time"-
-to devote to the study of problems and, presumably, to the making of suggestions here in this house which would help the government. These motions, the private bills or the public bills are not put forward merely for the personal satisfaction of any individual member. They are put forward here as part of the legitimate and proper business of this house.
On page 1729 Mr. Drew went on to say:
-this is the time to change the trend and to get back to a position where private members in this house are afforded the opportunity to assist the government by placing before parliament suggestions which are in keeping with the status of members as emphasized by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in his remarks in this house on at least two occasions.
What I have read indicates that when Mr. Drew was leader of the Conservative party in opposition he held very definite views on this subject. He had even more than that to say. I should like to refer hon. members to Hansard of April 28, 1952, at page 1639, where Mr. Drew is reported as having said:
This motion will have the effect of further limiting the rights of private members, which already have been limited greatly. During the years of war and immediately after the habit grew of setting aside the rules; but surely now we have reached a time when we can abide by the rules.
That was Hon. George Drew, sir, speaking on April 28, 1953. Let us bring it a little more up to date. Let us not deal just with a former leader of the Conservative party in opposition; let us deal with a former leader of the Conservative party in opposition who is now the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker). I refer you to Hansard of July 12, 1955, at page 5989, where the present Prime Minister in discussing a motion of a similar nature said:
The hon. member who preceded me mentioned the decline in the power of private members. That is all too true.
That is how he felt when the Liberals tried to curtail private members' days and rights, but he had a bit more than that to say. At page 5990 of Hansard of July 12, 1955, we find this statement:
One thinks of the Lauriers and the Bordens, and one could name other great speakers of that time who carried on debate for weeks on end, as a debate was recently carried on, for whenever the privileges and traditions of parliament are invaded parliament should be vocal.
The house may think before I am through that I am being a little bit vocal, but I am taking the advice of the Prime Minister

who, when he was leader of the opposition, said that when there is a motion to change a standing order and remove the rights of parliament, members should be vocal.
Now, sir, can we not all remember the righteous indignation of the present Minister of Finance when he sat on this side of the house, and what he had to say when the Liberals had the unmitigated temerity to try to remove any of the rights of the opposition and of private members, or to change a standing order that would affect us? Well, sir may we at this time just remind the Minister of Finance what his opinions were not so long ago, as recently as July 12, 1955, as found at page 5999 of Hansard:
This house cannot function without rules. The rules should be broad and fair.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Finance to listen to the next sentence.
Their purpose should be to safeguard particularly the rights of minorities in the house.
I hope the minister will not be disturbed because I gave only one quotation from him, but there are so many others of import that must be noted that I should like to refer to another stalwart of the rights of opposition minorities, and "do not change standing orders", and that is the Minister of Justice.

Perhaps I was unfair to the Minister of Finance in giving him only one quotation; I have two for the Minister of Justice:
Very often-and perhaps more so on this side than on the other-we members object to the way in

which the government seeks to control parliament, and to the way in which it ignores parliament.
You have the page number it you wish to check it. Or course you know, sir, when you ask for a suspension of standing orders to remove the rights of private members you are ignoring parliament. As I said, I have two quotations from the Minister of Justice but there are many more. My next quotation is found on page 5564 of Hansard of July 1, 1955, and reads as follows:
As a matter of fact, in connection with this whole matter I think the proper approach is that the rules are not a party matter. The rules do not belong to any party in the house and should not be changed by a majority vote of any party in the house.
This is a very important statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit an interruption? Is it not a fact that what was being discussed there was a change in the standing orders themselves, a change in the form of standing orders, a revision of the rules; and that in speaking of a change in the rules or to suggest that a change having permanent effect should not be imposed by a majority vote is very different from suggesting that a temporary suspension of a standing order be made without changing the rules, as is being done here?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what was being discussed in the House of Commons on July 1, 1955 was the second report of the special committee on procedure and consideration in committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Yes, a revision of the rules.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

That is right, but in my hon. friend's discussion of the rules he made this definite statement:
The rules do not belong to any party in the house and should not be changed by a majority vote of any party in the house.
If that principle is correct, Mr. Speaker, then we ask, on what basis does the same principle not apply to the changing of standing orders at the whim and the will of the government of which he is now a member? It is the same principle.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
The government is now going to make a change for their purposes in standing orders so that, starting next Monday, there will be no rights and privileges of private members in the house as far as their resolutions and bills are concerned. In other
Business of the House
words the discussion of private members' resolutions and bills is off as far as their rights are concerned.
I have a couple of more quotations. I am awfully sorry that the hon. member for Greenwood, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell) is not in his seat, because he was a fighter for the rights of minority parties and of private members. I hope the Postmaster General is not going to leave because I have a honey for him. I have always had great admiration for the hon. member for Greenwood, that wonderful person, outspoken and, I think, sincere. He had this to say on January 26, 1955, as found at page 559 of Hansard, when he was on this side of the house:
I stress again that what has happened is an almost complete negation of this principle. It is a kind of erosion of parliamentary rights. If we look at it clearly it is really a conspiracy against the principles of our constitution, and the Free Press is quite correct in what it states. We are told there is to be a further invasion of the rights of the minority. We are told that the rules are to be amended so that the rights we have had in the past will be drastically cut down. If this is attempted I can only hope that every member of the opposition, to whatever party he belongs, will resist to the utmost. I agree with facilitating the business in a sensible manner, but I think we should be astute to resist strongly anything which savours of merely cutting down the rights of the opposition, and I think we should do our very utmost to make the general public feel how important this is.
That was the view of the hon. member for Greenwood when on this side of the house at the time the standing orders were revised. I ask what is his position now, when we are faced with a further cutting down of the principles in the revised standing orders so far as the rights of minorities and of private members are concerned.
There is one more reference to the hon. member for Greenwood which I think is important. On February 8, 1955, as found on page 943 of Hansard, the hon. member for Greenwood said:
Let us remember this, with regard to ourselves in the opposition, that often we call ourselves watchdogs. But watchdogs should be able to growl and to bite. And if we are slipping into a situation where we do not growl and bite so well, then we ought to be very much on our guard, indeed.
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, are on our guard indeed in view of what we were told by the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers when they were in opposition and defending minorities and private members against the taking away of rights by the Liberals who now sit on this side of the house.
I also said there was one other minister whom I desired to quote, and that is the Postmaster General. I like him very much but I think, sir, that if I were to use the words he

Business of the House
used when the Liberals were taking away certain rights you would call me to order promptly. But I am not going to take that chance; I am going to quote from Hansard, which puts me completely in order. In view of the stand the Postmaster General took at that time, and in view of the position that as a member of the government he is taking now, I am going to ask him now whether he has the morality of an alley cat which he said the Liberals had when they tried to restrict the rights of private members.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: An alley rat.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

"Alley cat" was the term. As found at page 788 of Hansard of February 2, 1955, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace had this to say:
Under the British system, which is the one we follow in Canada, such cabinet tyranny can be cloaked in many ways. It will depend largely on the cleverness of the party in power in dissimulating its intentions and misleading the public as to whether or not the people generally realize the dangerous course their government may be following. When you have a government-
I am quoting, sir.
-that has the political morality of an alley cat and the lust for power of a Genghis Khan, it behooves those of us-and that includes all of us Conservatives on this side-who hold democracy precious to be on guard for all the people.
Now, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Louder.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: -I have tried to review not only the debates that took place in the house when the standing orders were revised in 1955 but also within the limits of time and to the best of my ability to review the statements as found in Hansard of such eminent men when in opposition as the former leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Drew, the present Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Justice and the Postmaster General to indicate how they felt when the then Liberal government endeavoured to take away any of the rights of minority parties under the standing orders or the rights of private members as related to the powers of the cabinet. In all my studies, Mr. Speaker, I have found that when on this side of the house members of the Conservative party were the champions of the maintenance of the rights of parliament, the rights of minority parties and the rights of private members.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

I think I have been quite honest in the quotations I have made, and I should like to ask those on the government side who applaud the stand the Conservative party took when in opposition how they,

with their terrific majority, can support the introduction of a motion which will take away certain rights and certain days provided for private members under the revised standing orders of the house. There is also a second part to the motion, but I am not going to go into any detail at the moment.

I refer to the stand taken by the Conservative opposition with regard to the difficulties of trying to do two jobs at one time, and the fact that the work of parliament should not be hastened.
I can remember, sir, and I know you can too, those speeches made on this side by Conservatives to the effect that our responsibilities did not have any time limit, and if we made laws they should have the proper consideration given to them.
Now, sir, I try to keep very closely to the record. I ask hon. members to consider what we have given them from the record. We ask also that the government give consideration to the withdrawal of the motion. But just in case they do not I should like to move an amendment. We will work extra hours if we have to, but we cannot go any further with the removal of the rights of parliament. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier):
That all the words beginning with "That notwithstanding" and ending with "as for Monday (government day), and" be struck out.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago I had the privilege of following the same two hon. members who have spoken today in a similar debate. At that time I endeavoured to point out to the Leader of the Opposition-there was no need to point it out to the hon. member for Vancouver East-that one of the great assets to being effective in opposition was to have something to whine about. Now, a few weeks later, we find that he has not learned that lesson.
As for the hon. member for Vancouver East, 1 have heard him make many dramatic and melodramatic speeches, but never more so than the one today, and never did he have less about which to be dramatic. If he used this same force and this same flow of words in support of a worthy cause he might get somewhere. But listening to him today, with all this torrent of words and all these quotations which had to do with an entirely different type of motion, one realized how little he needs protection in so far as the right to

speak in the House of Commons is concerned. Certainly no member, whether he be a member on the government side or a private member in either of the opposition parties, has so little to complain about in so far as taking the time of the house is concerned. I have no doubt that whether the house lasts for another three weeks, as we hope, or for another three months, the hon. member for Vancouver East will have his full share and more of the time that is spent in debate.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

They are more anxious than we are to get out of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) wants to get down to Newfoundland and sail his boat.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Unhappily, the minister is out of date.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: He has been wishing to get down there for weeks. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) wants to go back to Montreal to get started in his law practice. The Leader of the Opposition wants to get across the country mending fences, and that is a real job. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) wants to go to the Middle East and settle all the trouble there. I could go on-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: After listening to all this, you cannot say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, sit down; you had your say. I could go on with member after member in the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: You have not answered my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Your question was not worth answering, like most of the questions you ask.
Business of the House

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Does the minister mean to say they have such an effective gag that the backbenchers do not even dare say what they feel?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
I do not know of anybody in the house who would benefit more from a gag than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. It would increase his prestige immensely and at once.
Just look at the stand taken by these two parties, and this phony appeal they are making today. The Leader of the Opposition says, "Oh, it is quite all right to make further Mondays in this session government days; we have no objection." He is not worried about the rights of parliament or the rights of private members or the rights of anyone else when he is discussing the first part of this motion which is before the house today. He is objecting to sitting in the morning. The Liberals do not want to sit in the morning. Then we get over to the upper corner of the house-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: We are opposed to both.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: They do not object to sitting mornings.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, yes, we do; we do not like any part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Well, why did you move this amendment?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: We will explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: This is going to take quite a lot of explaining.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver East moves an amendment to delete only part of the motion which provides that further Mondays from now on will be devoted-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: This debate is not over yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: -to government days. One group does not want to sit in the morning, and the other one wants to have a chance to deal with private members' motions. The hon. member for Vancouver East made several statements about these private members' Mondays which were not accurate and which really shake the whole foundation of his argument. He said that if you took away these private members' Mondays, the private members would have no more rights; they could not bring in bills; they could not bring in motions, and he left the inference they would not even be able to talk.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
I did not.

Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: What are they fighting against? Private members' rights to bring in bills will not be interfered with in any way if this motion is carried.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Wait a minute; give me a chance. Private members still have the hour on Tuesday and Friday.
The only business which could be dealt with on a Monday if that day were to remain available to private members would be "Notices of Motions"-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: That is what I said; that is all day.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: -which appear on page 15 of today's order paper. As the hon. member knows, there are a number of these notices of motions on the order paper. That is the case in every session. Many of them are put there originally with the intention that they will get a little bit of publicity, but the members who put them there know very well that there will never be a debate on them.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Not ours; ours are for debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Already there have been five days devoted to private members' notices of motions in this session which has not yet lasted three months, and that has not been doing too badly. All that could have been discussed if these three remaining private members' Mondays had been made available would be the first three notices of motions now standing on the order paper at page 15.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: These motions can be discussed by the members when the estimates are up for consideration. For example, the first motion has to do with shipping Canadian goods through Canadian ports. There could be wide open discussion on that subject by the hon. member* for Halifax (Mr. Morris) if he wishes to discuss it when the estimates of the Department of Transport are before the house. The second one has to do with aid for education. That matter can be discussed when the estimates of the Department of Finance are under consideration, and I have not the slightest doubt that it will be discussed at that time and at great length.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
The third one has to do with setting up a system of credit facilities for agriculture and for fisheries. I believe that matter has already been discussed during the debate on [DOT] the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and it can be discussed further when the estimates of the Department

of Fisheries are before the house. Those are the only three resolutions which could come up even if there were three more private members' Mondays. When the hon. member for Vancouver East tries to make out that the government is riding roughshod over the rights of parliament and the rights of private members by the motion brought in today, he is just talking a lot of nonsense. The very fact that the Leader of the Opposition agrees that this is a reasonable course to follow I suggest makes the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver East look very weak.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Because they have not any resolutions; we have.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Then as to the morning sittings, may I say this. I am heartbroken about one statement made by the Leader of the Opposition. He said that the house leader was not giving him and the other members of the Liberal party reasonable notice of the business that was to come up in the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I hear them saying "hear, hear" to that statement, Mr. Speaker, particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. May I say that I have told him secrets all through the session. He has had more inside information than anybody else in the house.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: The minister had better be careful about what he is saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Why the hon. member should be shouting "hear, hear" today is more than I can say, except that he has acquired the habit. We have tried to give the opposition parties advance notice of the business that is to be brought before the house. I think in his heart each member across the way knows that is what we have been doing. I was the house leader for the official opposition for some years while Hon. Mr. Harris was the government house leader. We got along splendidly, just as do the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and I.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Wait and see. Don't speak too soon.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: If the hon. member has the nerve to rise in his place and accuse me of not letting him know what the business is to be, then I can say in advance that he will be talking through his hat.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Read some of your own
speeches that you made when you were over here on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
The hon. member did not quote my own speech. I do not think he has one.
The Leader of the Opposition has commented on the fact that committees are still sitting. He will agree, I am sure, that most of the committees have already reported. I do not believe that better committee work has ever been done than that which has been done in the present session. We took a new *course. We have referred the estimates of nine different departments to standing committees of the house. This is something that has never been done before. I do not believe there have ever previously been more than four or five departments whose estimates have been referred to committees. From my observation the members of the house serving on those committees, no matter to what party they belong, have done a splendid job. I believe this has been one of the finest accomplishments of the present session. It has been done in spite of the fact that a large proportion of the members of the house have had very little experience in parliamentary affairs.
It will be noted that we are not interfering with the committees during the whole of this week. The proposal is that the house start to sit on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday mornings next week, not this week. By that time all the committees will have reported, perhaps, with the exception of the public accounts committee and a special committee which will have to be set up to consider broadcasting legislation and possibly the committee on external affairs, although they have already had several sittings and I am hoping that they will be able to get their report in before the end of the week. We have very carefully deferred calling morning sittings until the work of the committees would be practically completed.
I do not believe there can be much real complaint about that course. Hon. members will notice further that we are not asking for a sitting on Wednesday evening. That time would be free even should this motion carry. I am sure I am expressing the belief of the majority of the members of each of the three parties in this house when I say the responsibility of this House of Commons now is to get the business of the session concluded just as quickly as possible, thereby letting the members get back to their constituencies.
This is not a regular type of session, as I pointed out on another occasion.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Oh, I do not suppose we shall ever have a regular type of session as long
Business of the House
as the hon. member is here. We hope to get the House of Commons back on a basis where a session can be called early in the new year and can deal with the business for that year before July 1. I see no reason why that could not be done in 1959.
I am hoping in spite of this debate today, which I know is not a debate from the heart so far as those across the way are concerned and, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has just said, neither is it a debate from the head-he said that, I would not have said it-that we can get down to business this week and finish everything off within the next three weeks. That would give members the opportunity to get home a week or ten days before-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Before the snow flies.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: -before the first of September. And I think it would be in the interests of every member and of the country as a whole if this were to be the result.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the house was quite wrong when he said a while ago that he did not think I would rise to protest the motion which has been made by the government as set out in the notice of motion now before the house. I am not rising to protest against the first part of the motion but certainly against the second part and to give my reasons for so doing.
The first part of the motion has to do with the amendment of standing order 15(3), and the house leader has indicated why he thinks there would be no objection to that. I believe I gave the house leader the reason for that decision on an earlier occasion; but my purpose in rising now is to protest-and to protest as vigorously as I can-that it is unconscionable, in my opinion, to begin sitting during the mornings, afternoons and evenings when the house has not before it a detailed plan of what the business is going to be from now until the end of the session. Are we going to sit for three weeks or six weeks under these conditions.
I think before this motion is passed we are entitled to know what the business is going to be. I am surprised that the house leader would refer to some of the private conversations which have taken place between us but, since he has done so it gives me an opportunity to refer to one of those conversations. Some time ago I said to the house leader, "What is the legislation which now remains to be dealt with before the end of the session", and without divulging his reply in detail he said there is this item

Business of the House
and there is that item; in other words, two items. I jotted them down, but a little later on he came back and said "I forgot; there are two more" and I jotted those two down. Still later he came over to my desk and said, "Oh, I forgot another one." That makes five.
What, then, is the position? I think it will be agreed that, when the hon. members who are sitting on the other side of this house now sat on this side and asked the then leader of the government what the business of the house was under circumstances such as these, the then government leader put the business on the record in Hansard, so that we knew what it was. It is one thing to say "Everything that is in the speech from the throne" is the remaining business; and quite another to detail what that legislation is to be.
As I say, I think before we are asked to approve this motion we should be told item by item, what the motions and these bills are to be, and we should not be told in a general way, such as we have been told by the Prime Minister when he was asked this question by the Leader of the Opposition, that "it is everything contained in the speech from the throne". We are entitled to greater detail than we have been given.
The leader of the house began by stating that we on this side of the house had nothing to say, that we were whining. I do not know of any greater whiner than the leader of the house, particularly when he sat on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, but it was good whining.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I will not do him the discourtesy of referring to what a former colleague of mine ascribed to him, because while I think the words fitted him accurately it would none the less depart from the general spirit of this debate to do so. I will however refer to something else, because the house leader has said as part of his great oration that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate wanted to get back to his ship. He does not have a ship; he has lost it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
That is not all he
has lost.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: He has also said the hon. member for Essex East wants to go to the Middle East. I do not know whether or not that is true, but I do know one thing; if he did go there he would do an excellent job.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: He as also said the hon. member for Laurier wants to get back to his law practice.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: That would be a good idea.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I shall not comment on that other than to say that one of the friends of the house leader told me one day "You know this man Green does not want to get out to his constituency at all. He likes the house so much he wants to sit here morning, afternoon and evening. There is nothing he loves better than the House of Commons. Why should he go back to his constituency?" I am beginning to realize now that this friend of his was quite correct when he made that statement, but let me tell the leader of the house that we on this side of the house are prepared to stay here as long as it is necessary to do the business of the house.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Furthermore, much as I would like to get back to my practice which I have not looked after now for many, many months, I do not wish to do so until the business of the house has been terminated. Let me further tell the leader of the house that if we knew that from now until the end of the session we would have certain definite pieces of legislation to face and exactly what was going to be brought down, then I think it would make our position much easier and much clearer with reference to this motion.
This we have not been told. Our position the other day with reference to the first morning sittings was entirely different from our position today, because we then saw that the end of the session was in the offing. Now that we are getting nearer to the end of the session, surely we should be told what is the business of the house. That is why we on this side of the house protest the second aspect of this resolution and will continue to do so until we know the business of the house.
Furthermore the leader of the house said something about the work of the committees. I am not in a position to know what is the progress of that work. The house leader has not told us. All he did was make a sweeping statement that the work was proceeding well, but I do not know that I can agree with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Most of them have reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
I do not think I can agree
with the statement he has made that this new idea is working out so well. As a matter of fact I do not think it is, and I may say that I hope he will not repeat the mistake which I respectfully suggest was made in submitting the estimates to the committees. I do not want to go into the details of what happens in some of those committees, but

I do not think they are doing efficient work.
I think if the estimates had remained in the house and if ministers had been here to reply, rather than having their officers reply in their stead in committee it would have been much more efficient, and I believe the work of the house would have proceeded much faster.
The house leader has said that he has taken us into his confidence and repeatedly told us what the business would be. Yes, he has, for one or two or sometimes three days, but I cannot remember-and in this I may be mistaken-one occasion during this session when he has given us notice of what was going to take place for one week in advance. That was something which often was done by the former minister of finance-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Over and over again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
I say without fear of contradiction that when I sat on the other side of the house the previous minister of finance repeatedly gave the business of the house for a full week in advance. We are now being denied knowledge of what the business will be from now until the end of the session. We are told for one day and two days and we are often told, as the house leader has said, to use his own words "I will give you notice for Monday and Tuesday, but I do not know what it is going to be on Wednesday". It is difficult enough for a group such as we are in the opposition to get ready for the business with a week's notice in advance. How much more difficult is it going to be when we have only one or two days' notice?
I conclude by saying that before this motion passes the house is entitled to far more information on the business that lies ahead of us from now until the end of the session than it has received up to the present time; and until it gets that information I submit, as others have stated, that this motion should be withdrawn.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this motion is wrong in two aspects. If it is passed it will wipe out three private members' Mondays, and will also call for morning sittings every day. We have been asked today whether or not the arrangements for the various committees of this house are working well. There have been slated for this afternoon meetings of the committee on external affairs and the committee on agriculture, while the house is meeting. As long as the government has a great many committees meeting while the house is sitting I submit it is impossible for hon. members to do an efficient job in the committees as
Business of the House
well as in the house. The practice now being suggested makes a farce not only of the committees but also of parliament itself.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech by the Minister of Public Works, who is a most entertaining speaker. If the Prime Minister has an understudy in terms of his particular method of speaking, an understudy who has learned his part well, it is the Minister of Public Works. By making use of his excellent sense of humour and by displaying his wide smile when he is really putting it to you, the Minister of Public Works is apparently able to argue effectively on both sides of the question.
When he started to roast the members of the official opposition he said, "Ah, I know why you are in favour of the first part of the motion. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wants to go sailing a boat, the hon. member for Laurier wants to go back to his law practice and the hon. member for Essex East wants to go over to the Middle East"-for the hon. member for Essex East to be going to the Middle East seems strangely fitting-"and the Leader of the Opposition wants to go on a political tour that is very much needed." The Minister of Public Works was making extremely important points in his humorous fashion.
When he came to the other part of the matter and explained why the government was doing this, what did he say? He said it is the responsibility of the government to get the session concluded as quickly as possible so that hon. members could get back to their constituencies.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out that I said it was the responsibility of the members.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: That is not the way I took it. The minister may feel it is the responsibility of the members, but here we have a motion which has been introduced by the Prime Minister and which has been spoken to by the house leader. The motion bears the stamp of approval of the government, and its purpose as explained by none other than the Minister of Public Works is to enable hon. members to get back to their constituencies, and to help the four hon. gentlemen in the Liberal party to whom he referred with such humour to do the very things he was scolding them for wanting to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: You want to get back too, do you not?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first interest here, as I believe is the first interest of all hon. members of the C.C.F. group, is to see that we do our part in promoting

Business of the House
legislation which we believe is in the best interests of the ordinary people in this country-
Mr. Pallet!: The C.C.F. members are great promoters, all right.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: -and in conducting the affairs of this house efficiently and in accordance with the rules. In order to efficiently conduct the affairs of the nation in this house it is not necessary that we put on a steamroller in order to wind up the session within two or three weeks. No less an authority than a former speaker of this house who has already been quoted said, as reported in the Journals of this house for December 1947, that a two-month session if it is mismanaged is more wasteful of time than a six-month session during which no time has been lost.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Who said that? Was that the Minister of Public Works?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
No; Mr. Speaker Fauteux, who was the speaker of this house at that time.
I was exceedingly disappointed in the official statement made by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that his party would not object to that part of the motion which would eliminate the three private members' Mondays. The right of private hon. members to present motions under the heading of notices of motion and to expect a substantial number of these motions to come up during the course of a session is a tradition of long standing in this house. This is the first session in my memory when it has apparently been the official position of the government to talk out all private members' motions. We might be able to deal with more than three motions before the session concluded if the house leader did not take the attitude he took this afternoon, that only three motions could be dealt with on three further private members' Mondays.
Although this government has the greatest majority that any government in the history of this country has had it is apparently more terrified than were governments in the past of having motions or bills introduced by private members brought to a vote. No matter what the motion may be, no matter how innocuous its wording may be, no matter if it comes from a government supporter, the official position of this government is to put on one Conservative speaker after another to talk out the motions. That is the situation no matter how government members may attempt to paint it.
The greatest folly of all is that the government by this device is seeking to take away from the House of Commons the right of private hon. members to three private

members' Mondays, a right which is embodied in the rules of this house. I was amazed and disappointed at the argument advanced by the Minister of Justice to the effect that the government is not taking so much away because this does not represent a revision of the rules. It is certainly to be hoped that this is neither a revision of the rules nor a precedent, because hon. members of the government as well as many hon. members of the Liberal party in this house know that over the years there have often been more than six private members' Mondays or two private members' Thursdays, and that the rule in the rule book today was placed there because it was the recommendation of a committee of this house representative of all parties, which met in 1955. By agreement and unanimous vote the committee decided that it would be better to provide for a fixed number of private members' Mondays than to leave it to chance.
What is the government attempting to do? The government is introducing a motion to take away the right of hon. members of this house to three further private members' Mondays. This motion interferes with an important right of private members. Something the government should avoid like the plague is any suggestion that the cabinet is dictating the rules of procedure and the rights of this house. The motion before us this afternoon is more than a motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister. This motion is the result of a cold, calculated decision on the part of the cabinet to eliminate three private members' Mondays.
I say to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and to the members of the government that standing order 15 has become the plaything of the cabinet; that the whole rule book and our whole procedure in this house are in jeopardy.
I had thought the Minister of Public Works, when he made the strong statement which he made when in opposition, would carry those beliefs into the cabinet, but apparently they were to be just statements from the sounding board of the opposition, and once the party has landed in the seats of the mighty then the means by which they obtained power cease to have little concern, because the Minister of Public Works is doing now precisely what he condemned for so many years.
I think it goes even farther than that.
I think the minister indicated this afternoon that he does not know exactly what is in the rule book because he said that as far as this is concerned all it will do is wipe out three private members' notices of motions. Well, of course, that is not all it does because

the fourth, fifth and sixth Mondays are different from the first, second and third Mondays. They are different in this respect. In addition to the notices of motions for the production of papers on the fourth, fifth and sixth Mondays, private bills are next in the order of precedence. Therefore, the government is not, as the minister says, merely taking away the motions of three private members.

You are not worrying very

I am not opposed to that bill being defeated but even if I am opposed to the measure passing this house, the rules of the house should be maintained. If in the maintenance of the rules a private bill passes this house to which I am opposed, then that is the way it should be. When the Minister of Public Works sat in another position on this side of the house he said this on March 23, 1954, as reported on page 3216 of Hansard:
The Progressive Conservative party stands for the supremacy of parliament. That has been one of our fundamental beliefs down through the years. We believe in parliament being supreme rather than
Business of the House
the cabinet, and we believe that only in that way can we have a free parliament in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

The Minister of Public Works speaks of parliament being free but this motion was presented to parliament following a cabinet meeting. Is that the way to keep parliament free, to destroy the rule book, to destroy our standing orders, because the cabinet has decided that the first responsibility of members should be to get back to their constituencies. I think that is an untenable position; I think the government is making a grave mistake in presenting this motion at this time.
In spite of the statement which was made hurriedly by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I suggest that the official opposition will be sorry indeed in the days that lie ahead if on this day they share with the government the responsibility of taking away some of the fundamental rights of this parliament as incorporated in the motion of the Prime Minister brought in at this time. The only position for any opposition group to take is to say that the rule book by which members' rights are guaranteed shall not be tampered with except by agreement, except by unanimous consent. But when any party or any members object there should be no motion of the cabinet to turn on the party whips and force such a motion through the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister has been most eloquent in his stand in opposing closure, and I agree with him. I think a motion to abolish closure is one that should be put through this house and become part of our rules; but if it were possible to apply a closure motion to a private member's notice of motion it would not kill the motion, it would not destroy it; it would merely say that at one o'clock in the morning following the day of debate the vote shall be taken. But this motion which is now before us places private members' motions in a much inferior position. Closure is not being applied which limits debate and brings on a vote. This kind of closure is an eradication of the debate; it is a removal of the notice of motion on the order paper.
In an important publication entitled "Parliament and the People", issued by the Progressive Conservative party national headquarters, 141 Laurier avenue west, Ottawa, Ontario, the following quotation is found on page 9. It is entitled "No Pipe Dream" and reads as follows:
I have seen the progressive restriction of the supremacy of parliament in the last 10 years. I have seen parliament bludgeoned, and I say that is no pipe dream. Bludgeoned by a majority. I have seen the hands of the cabinet directing members and disciplining them into an abject servility.

Business of the House
That is the Prime Minister. I ask him to take off the party whip, to remove from the motion that part of it which eradicates three private members' Mondays, and therefore helps destroy the very foundation of the House of Commons, namely our rules and procedures.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take only two or three minutes to deal with one aspect of this problem which has not been mentioned to date. I might say briefly that after listening to the Minister of Public Works this afternoon I think he has become quite skilled in the use of the axe, the shovel and the rake. No wonder he is Minister of Public Works.
Other members of this group have dealt with the constitutional, the procedural and the legal aspects of the loss of the rights of parliament in this motion doing away with private members' days. They have all done very well indeed and I am not going to repeat what they had to say, but I do want to say that as far as my experience in this house is concerned over a period of 13 years it seems to me that the parliament of Canada has been in existence for 91 years and to date has failed to organize its business and its work in a logical and satisfactory manner.
With respect to the hours, I want to make two points. The lengthened hours of the sitting of this house make it impossible for members to attend to their duties properly, to give satisfactory attention to legislation on the order paper, legislation that may come forward or to the estimates. I think this argument is of double force, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that at the present time we still have a number of committees sitting and one or two of those committees are sitting two or three times a day while the house is sitting.
But I rise, particularly, Mr. Speaker, to say that those lengthened hours over a long number of weeks are particularly unfair to the staff of the House of Commons.
The disorganized manner in which our business is being handled means that the staff of the House of Commons have had their holidays completely disorganized. Many of them are without the opportunity to enjoy summer holidays with their children during the months when their children are on holiday from school. Other members of the staff are required to put in unnecessarily long and unfair hours, but before resuming my speech I want to mention particularly the strain that these very long days impose on the Hansard reporters. We all know that repeatedly they are required to stay here until after midnight preparing the typescript so
'Mr. Argue.]
that Hansard can be published the next day. In addition, it is very unfair to what I term our Hansard angels, the ladies who type for the Hansard reporters. These young ladies find it a very difficult time because of the lengthening of the hours over a long period. I do think that in future sessions we must consider the welfare of the staff of the House of Commons. Finally, I hope that the situation that exists today and the debate we are having will result in better organization of the business of the House of Commons in the future.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the house that I too will only be a limited number of minutes. However, I think this is a vital matter. The last time a motion extending the hours of sitting was presented I think the reason was possibly understandable. However, the present motion invades the rights of private members with respect to notices of motions and I feel that the opposition would be failing in its responsibility if it did not sound a warning.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) claims that he knows the wishes of the opposition members and that those wishes are identical with the wishes of other members, that opposition members also would like to reach an early end to this session. If such is the case I must ask the Minister of Public Works why he did not consult with the opposition before the government made the decision it obviously has made.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS

No, it was not. The opposition was advised of the decision of the cabinet. The opposition was not consulted before the cabinet made its decision. If there must be amendments to our standing orders I feel that there should be rather wide consultation because they are very important rules in our parliamentary institution. There should be such consultation before the cabinet makes up its mind and not consultation afterwards.
I was also very alarmed by the statement of the minister, which I hope was made inadvertently, that at the most three resolutions would be dealt with. If he meant what he said it indicates that the government has made up its mind that it is going to use the weight of a political party in the determination of what is to happen to private members' motions. I cannot fail but be alarmed when I see in country after country, even in Canada, the growth of power of political machines. I think we should watch that very carefully. I know that the Conservative party is not alone in having such a fault. I think

it obtains in all political parties in Canada. A belief is developing that the party in power and the party machine and organization must have their way and in my opinion that is regrettable regardless of where we find it. The minister's statement that we could take only three resolutions in three days is an indication that the government is also afflicted with the power of the party concept.
The minister made a considerable point of the fact that we can discuss these problems when the estimates are dealt with. With reference to federal aid for education he said that he did not doubt at all that we would be taking a good deal of the time when discussing the estimates of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to discuss federal aid for education. If the minister is sincere in his contention that all these subjects can be amply aired on the estimates, then I must ask the minister why we need this motion at all because it is obvious that the number of motions we will be able to deal with will be limited by the mere fact that only three more Mondays are available. Yet if the minister is inviting members of the house to speak on the subject matters of all the various motions when considering estimates I can assure the minister that he will lose far more than the three days he is now hoping to gain. Surely if he says to members of the house that the government is going to take away three days but members can spend all the time they like on the estimates he is not arguing very successfully for any progress in the direction that it is indicated is desirable.
I should like to point out to the house that the subject matters of these motions are important indeed. The government introduces its ideas in the speech from the throne and other members of the House of Commons should have a chance to air their views. I have looked over the list of notices of motion and most of them deal with very vital matters that need airing. Federal aid for education is only one. Others include pensions, the difficulties of the textile industry, the need for further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, human rights, conservation of our natural resources, highways, the marketing of coal, a coast guard service, industrial decentralization, the elections act, the dumping of foreign agricultural products on our markets, Canada's one hundredth birthday, a municipal loan fund, lotteries and the employment of men over the age of 45.
Finally, I must remind the house that this year the house sat for the first month, January, and then reconvened in the middle of May. If the minister's wish is realized it will end about the middle of August. This adds up to a total of four months. This urgent
Business of the House
need to complete the business of parliament and get home is not going to be looked upon very kindly by the people of Canada when they realize that we were at our job in parliament for only four months of the whole year while still collecting our pay for 12 months. I can quite understand that when the house begins to sit in the first month of the year, members then work for seven or eight months and the end of July is passed and we reach the middle of August, as has happened before, members should feel that they should end the session and go home for a while to consult with their people. However, when we have only spent four months here and there are so many urgent matters needing the attention of parliament as indicated in these notices of motion, then I feel that we are neglecting our duties.

be horrified at being compared with the gentleman named in this press clipping, but I should like them to stop and think for one moment about how big a step they are taking along the road outlined in this clipping by the present resolution. This press clipping is from Lisbon and reads:

I believe that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) speaks he will close the debate and I would therefore like first to make two very brief observations. We voted against the amendment because, among other things, we felt that by voting for the amendment we would have been implying that we were in favour of the second part of the proposition which is that part of which we have an unalterable objection. It seemed to us, therefore, that we would have looked rather ridiculous to vote for the striking out of one half of the proposition leaving the other.
So far as the main proposition is concerned-the second paragraph of the motion- we continue to be thoroughly opposed to this at the present time. It may be that before the end of the session it will be appropriate to do as was done when we were in office at a point where it was really possible to see the end of the session, and that is to ask the house to sit on every morning of the week.
We do, however, have many items of major legislation, according to all the indications, which have to be introduced in this house; items of legislation which, if the government carries them out, certainly ought to go to the

committees to receive very careful consideration. That would mean that this session will continue four or five more weeks, at the very least, if we are to do our duty conscientiously. It would seem to me quite ridiculous, therefore, to ask the house at this very early date to do something which the previous administration did only at the very end of the session when virtually nothing remained to be dealt with but the estimates.
As the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said, we do not even know what legislation the government intends to introduce and I hope the Prime Minister will, if he speaks, give the house a detailed account of that legislation. Unless the government is going to throw overboard practically its whole program, I still think it is far too early in the session to be asking us to undertake hours of this kind and I hope the Prime Minister will indicate to us what legislation is still forthcoming and that he will leave no doubt in our minds that this session will not be closed without the implementation of the report of the royal commission on the revision of the terms of union with Newfoundland.
