speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a most interesting debate, one that has revealed many intriguing facets of the beliefs of the parties opposite with respect to parliament
Business of the House
and the manner in which parliament should discharge its responsibilities.
I am not going to go into a great deal of detail, but I would like to say that I would have placed before the house at the very beginning the entire legislative program but, before I was in a position to rise-and there is no criticism inherent in these words I am about to utter-the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) rose and commenced his address.
I must say, however, that as I listened to the hon. gentlemen sitting to your immediate left-the members of the C.C.F. party and in particular as I listened to their authorities on the constitutional system of this country quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch)-I thought how applicable were the words of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) when he inferentially referred to inconsistency. I could not help but recall, while the hon. member for Vancouver East was enunciating those great principles of parliamentary government, a speech he made on November 10, 1943, in which he said when they get power they are going to "scrap the British North America Act".

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
And when it was suggested to him that he may have been misquoted, he made it very clear that he had not been misquoted. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) spoke of the few days during which parliament had sat and how much there was to do. The reason why I rise to deal with that particular matter is that I do not want to allow the people of Canada to conclude that parliament has not been sitting very continuously since October 14 last, or that there has been any neglect of responsibility on the part of parliament. Even making due allowance for the election and the campaign of several months which intervened, of the 295 days since October 14, 1957, parliament has sat on 142 days. That answers the hon. gentleman who tried to leave the impression that parliament had but one concern, namely to go home, when as a matter of fact I doubt that there has been any period of 295 days, except during wartime, in which parliament has sat for 142 days.
It has been very interesting to listen to my hon. friends to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, for they have endeavoured by constant repetition to delude the people of Canada into believing that they are in fact the true opposition because each and every one in that group speaks on each and every occasion and opportunity. I realize the difficulty of my hon. friends over there. They

Business of the House
speak of how difficult it is to attend the various committee meetings but certainly we cannot accept the responsibility for the diminution in the degree to which the representation in that quarter since March 31 does not permit membership on all the committees of the House of Commons.
I was so much surprised to hear the suggestion made that the committee system was not working out very well. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said that but whether he was going into the question with the same degree of care that he usually employs, I do not know. All I can say is this. In my experience-and while I did not come to this house as early as did the hon. member for Laurier-in the time I have been here I have never seen any group of parliamentarians apply themselves with a greater care and attention in the committees of parliament than I have seen this year. As a matter of fact, I speak as one who is not a very good committee man. Over the years I have more or less cast out on the efficacy of the committee system. However, others whose experience is wider as committee members than is my own were able to convince me that the committee system could indeed be incorporated into our system without borrowing anything from the constitutional position of the congress of the United States. I think the committee system has worked out very well.
My hon. friend said that if we had not had the committees on estimates we would have discussed these things in the house. I would point out that there has never been any delay here. There has never been a day on which parliament has not been in control of the order paper. There has always been legislation and there have always been the necessary estimates available from the very beginning of the session. When the Leader of the Opposition speaks about organizing parliament, all I can say is that if there has been any lack of organization it has not been on this side. We have had legislation available and ready for the house at all times. We have had the estimates available. It has been difficult I know in connection with the estimates to put into one session almost the complete estimates of two years but always there has been a legislative program. When the hon. member for Laurier said that in the past we used to know a week in advance what was coming, I can only comment that I do not think I was here in those days.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I was and I remember it quite well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
After all, all that anyone asks is that he knows reasonably well, within a matter of two or three days, the general

program and that course and that objective have been the objective and course of this government. It has not been due in any way to indolence, a lack of diligence or a lack of placing the legislative program before parliament that in a period since October 14 we have sat in session 45 per cent of the actual sitting days.
I know there are changes that could be made in parliament. The hon. member for Vancouver East referred to a speech that I made in the House of Commons on July 12, 1955. That was when the special committee on procedure was before the house for discussion. We were dealing with the necessity of preserving under general rules the conduct of parliament in a proper way. I pointed out on that occasion, and I am not going to say today that I have changed my views in that connection, that it is difficult with desks before us to achieve that degree of perfection in debate, cogency in argument and lack of prolixity which is so necessary for effective debate. We are all guilty. I know that someone will say if I did not have a desk before me at this moment I should not be able to have these two books before me.
The fact remains that one of the major reasons the British parliament has been so effective is that there are no desks before the members of that house that permit of an extensiveness in extemporaneousness aided and abetted by manifold documents on a desk. They speak there after preparation. They have no space on an individual desk before them on which to lay voluminous notes or great volumes. When a speaker has to bend every now and then in order to remove books and papers from under the seat upon which he was sitting prior to his rising to take part in the debate he is less inclined to have copious reference to voluminous documents.
When my hon. friends to the left of the Speaker say that the rights of parliament are being interfered with because each and every one of them will not have the right to speak over and over again, may I invite them to take a look at the parliament at Westminster and realize the degree to which that parliament has a wide complexity of subjects with which to deal and also realize the fact that there in debate a number are chosen of those who will speak on the basis of the motion of the Speaker after discussion with the Whips and there is no unnecessary repetition or redundancy. There are no 40-minute speeches. And yet the gentlemen in that parliament in the course of a session get through a tremendous amount of legislative enactment and discussion.
If it is to discharge its responsibility parliament must be more than a place where repetitious utterance masquerades as wisdom. I

think there is a great deal to be said in favour of the suggestion of my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition that we can do much to reorganize parliament to make it effective. There is much that all of us can do in this regard for if we really give our testimony truly not all of us are free from being offenders. We can make this house more effective not by extending to the point of view of having parliament sit throughout the entire year but in another way.
I believe that consideration might be given at the next session, after consultation, to adding to the changes that were made in 1955. On the basis of experience, without in any way interfering with the freedom of speech which must remain in parliament actually as theoretically, we might achieve an increased degree of efficiency through reorganization along the lines I have suggested to bring this parliament and the discussions of this parliament generally in consonance with the experience and practice of the mother of parliaments. There the voice of freedom has never been silent as a result of that political experience which is peculiarly that of the British and which ensures the maintenance of freedom through speech while at the same time preventing unnecessary repetition which can only lengthen the sessions of parliament without in any way contributing to the benefit of legislation.
I think some effective changes were made in 1955. I just look back at some of the remarks I made at that time. There was a time in the old House of Commons when members spoke for four or five hours. They did not by speaking at that length really add too much after the first 20 minutes to assist in the solution of problems. Some hon. members will recall that in 1912 a very famous member from the city of Montreal spoke for 11J hours. Then he said, "Mr. Speaker, I am coming to the essence of what I want to place before this house." Those were the happy days. In 1885, at the time of the rebellion, great debates took place in the old House of Commons. As I recall it-and I am speaking entirely from recollection-the first four or five who spoke took no less than four hours each. That did not make parliament any more effective.
When the discussions took place at the time the rules were changed to provide for speeches of 40 minutes as a maximum for members other than those designated, there were many who said that this was a grave interference with the freedom of parliament. Again, a couple of years ago, when speeches in committee were reduced to 30 minutes, there were some who might have felt that
Business of the House
the reduction would make some difference in the solution of our problems; but in the light of experience I do not think that has been found to be so.
When hon. members say that parliament has not had a chance to speak and that we have changed since we came over here I simply give this answer once more. There have been 295 days since October 14, and parliament has sat 142. When they say that it is really terrible, the loss of private members' days, I say that there have been five so far and there were private members' days last fall as well. Members of the opposition were perfectly willing at that time to reduce the number of private members' days. As I recall it, the hon. member for Laurier said that it was only late in the session that similar motions were made before. I have the record here. In 1956, morning sittings continued from July 16 to August 14, four weeks and two days. I think, generally, that has been approximately the time at which the adoption of morning sittings has been accepted by the house.
I have been asked to say something in regard to the program in general. I am not going to read over the list on the order paper, except to say that the items on the order paper will be taken up and, I hope, passed by the house. With regard to those matters that appear in the speech from the throne, in view of the degree to which there has been some controversy in northern Alberta as to the site of the railroad to Slave lake, we feel further consideration should be given to that and will not have that legislation in respect of the building of a railway before the house at this session.
What is the remainder of the record? There is the bill of rights, the bill to amend the broadcasting act, the legislation respecting agriculture in general and the South Saskatchewan dam, the bill to provide for the building of the Campobello and Maine bridge by sharing among the United States government, the province of New Brunswick and the government of Canada; the bill to amend the Customs Act in one detail referred to in the budget speech; and, of course, a bill respecting supply in 1957-58, in pursuance of the undertaking given by myself during the recent election campaign, as well as an amendment to the citizenship act.
Now, sir, good progress has been made-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) as to whether or not the government had received an appeal from Canadians of Polish descent through the Canadian-Polish congress of Canada, and had protested to the Polish government concerning the violation by their police of the holy Catholic shrine at the monastery of Czestochowa.
A communication dated August 1 has been received which reads as follcws:
Toronto, Ontario August 1, 1958.
Right Honourable John Diefenbaker,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
Profoundly moved by the information received about the search of the monastery of Czestochowa, July 21, and recent campaign against the Catholic church in Poland, we appeal to you on behalf of the 250,000 Canadians of Polish descent to raise on behalf of the Canadian government and in parliament a most serious protest against the brutal attack upon the most holy shrine of Poland and religious freedom by a totalitarian and godless regime.
Head Executive board, Canadian Polish Congress.
News reports indicate that since Saturday and also during the previous few days discussions have been carried on between the state of Poland and the church authorities in Warsaw and that certain agreements have been reached. Naturally this action by the Polish police is disturbing and the appeal that is directed to me is one that has my utmost sympathy. However, in view of the fact that this matter is now being considered as between the authorities to which I have referred the Canadian government does not propose to take any action which might have the

Inquiries of the Ministry appearance of interference with the arrangements which apparently have been made or are about to be arrived at. Naturally, too, the government wants to be assured that there shall be no impairment of that degree of tolerance and truce that has prevailed between the church and state in Poland in recent months and we hope that as a result of these communications that are passing between those I have mentioned, the state and the church, the future result will be a maximum degree of religious freedom.
I feel that at this time any action taken by this government by way of protest would add nothing to the solution of the problem when a solution is apparently being arrived at in consequence of deliberations as between the interested parties.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ACTIVITIES TO HALT VIOLENCE IN INTERIOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the R.C.M. Police, as the house is aware, has contracts with eight provinces in Canada, and under those contracts and arrangements pursuant thereto they are also responsible for the policing of some 120 municipalities. I think that normally it would not be expected that the Minister of Justice here would enter into detailed replies on the orders of the day with regard to incidents in connection with the policing of a municipality which is governed by the contract in effect in that regard. However, in this particular case, because of the unusual nature of the incidents, I think it is appropriate that I should give an answer.
I am informed that the strength of the R.C.M. Police in Prince Rupert, as governed by the terms of the contract, is 18 men from April 1 to September 30, and 16 for the remainder of the year. That is the number of men devoted to municipal policing. Saturday, August 2, marked the windup of the British Columbia centennial celebrations in Prince Rupert. I should also say I am advised that the fishing fleet was in harbour. Altogether, according to my advice, there were some three or four thousand visitors in the city on that day. During the evening, some 10 arrests were made by the police, and with the final two arrests for drunkenness and fighting a crowd of some 800 gathered and started to throw bottles and stones at the police. This uproar continued and a crowd followed the police to the police station and the city hall area. They continued to demonstrate there and to shout and throw stones. At 1.15 a.m. on Sunday, the third of August, the mayor read the riot act. It had no effect. He read it a second time, with apparently the same results.
In the meantime the crowd continued to shout and throw stones and bottles which broke windows in the city hall, in the police station and in some of the stores. At 1.30 in the morning the police, feeling that further action was necessary, moved in with tear gas. At about 2.30 in the morning, as a result of this action, they had managed to get the
Inquiries of the Ministry crowd dispersed and the situation under reasonable control. In the course of those incidents some policemen were injured, but only two in any serious fashion. There were also two people amongst the crowd that had taken part in the demonstration who were hurt sufficiently seriously to be hospitalized. I am advised, however, that they were not seriously injured.
In the course of these incidents 22 people were arrested for unlawful assembly and I am advised that the prosecuting attorney is now drafting charges. I am further advised that conditions today are quiet and have been ever since the crowd was dispersed. I am further advised that the city council met in emergency meeting immediately after the riot and fully endorsed the action taken by the police.
Now, with regard to the alleged activities on the part of the United States coastguard, I am advised that the U.S.S. Balsam had brought the mayor and some other dignitaries from Ketchikan, Alaska, to take part in this final day of the celebration. The ship was in harbour at the time but it is not clear, on the basis of the most recent information I have been able to obtain, whether the shore patrol from the Balsam were engaged in their normal patrol activities regarding the supervision of their own personnel who were on shore or whether in fact they participated, or were requested to participate, to any greater extent in controlling the outbreak. I would therefore prefer not to make any further statement on that matter until I have more detailed reports.

The Prime Minister also made some very interesting observations this afternoon about changes in the atmosphere, in the procedure, in the physical facilities of the chamber which might speed up our debates and make them more effective, and for that purpose he thought that there was perhaps something to be said for taking away our desks. He was good enough the other day to offer me, and perhaps one or two other privileged members, loudspeakers in our offices so we could do two jobs at once, the work in the office and the work on the floor of the house, but I hope he is not making that offer on condition that if we accept it it will be a kind of compensation for losing our desks. I know, of course, as the Prime Minister pointed out, how tempting it is to pile up book on book on our desks but I assure my hon. friend that the books I have piled up here are for the purpose of making my notes a little easier to read and not to quote from. I will do my best on this occasion to reconcile what he called the necessity for progress with the temptation to prolixity, and my right hon. friend speaks, I think, with some authority on that matter.

speechtext:
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that in the absence of any denial on the part of the government concerning the accuracy of the press report the people of this country will accept these excerpts as genuine and accurate, and the fact that they contradict in some respects the economic and financial prospects for 1958 made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech is going to cause a great deal of uneasiness in this country. I suggest that it is time for the government to clear up this matter. I repeat that the only way this can be done, the only way the government can show it has good faith and can brand these excerpts as inaccurate, if it wants to, is by tabling this report. I have said it twice before and I will say it again. It is regrettable because this is not the course that should be followed in connection with a report of this kind, a confidential and secret report from government officials to their ministers. But I also-say once again that the person on whom the blame must rest for the fact that the report should be tabled and that it should be done in this way and for the fact that the whole system of economic reporting is now prejudiced is the Prime Minister himself.
The damage was done last January, Mr. Speaker. It was done for partisan, political purposes when carefully selected excerpts from a confidential report which had not up to that time ever been made public were read by the Prime Minister in this house. The foundation of confidence in the procedure that had existed over the years was weakened as a result of that. What followed since January 20 was a depressing but natural development stemming from that original misdeed. And the result of that, has been that a system of economic reporting confidential, admirable, essential for the formulation of economic policy has been weakened, I hope not beyond repair. The entire system of economic reporting has now been prejudiced. That, Mr. Speaker, is the main burden of our attack on the government in this matter. That underlines their irresponsibility.
It was easy for the Prime Minister last January 20 to pick up this report and remove the cover which was marked confidential and take out a few excerpts to prove his particular points and thus make contents of the report public. He knew perfectly well- and if he did not he should have known it-

Canadian Economic Outlook that this was a report that was not meant to be made public. He knew perfectly well-and again if he did not he should have known it-that it was a confidential report used by the government in making its economic calculations. If it was right for the Liberal government to maintain the confidential character of the 1957 report at that time it is right for this government to maintain the confidential character of the 1958 report. But if the Liberal government erred-and that is a mild word-and if the Liberal government is to be condemned and castigated for not making the report of 1957 public, what can we say about a government that in the light of all the existing circumstances and in the light of all the speculation, misunderstanding, uncertainty, doubt and confusion that has been caused by the excerpts that have appeared in print from this report refuses to make the original report public; when the members of that government deny any knowledge of the report let alone any excerpts in the press from it? And so, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the actions of the government in connection with 'The Canadian Economic Outlook' have seriously weakened the value of confidential advice from civil servants with resultant damage to the proper formulation of economic and fiscal policies."

Is your mind not transported back, Mr. Speaker, to the 20th day of January, the Leader of the Opposition making his maiden speech in the house after his election at the Liberal convention the week before, leading charge after charge against the treasury benches, charge after charge? Then, Mr. Speaker, you remember that he followed it up with an amendment that was so extraordinary that he could not even keep a straight face himself in reading it to the house. And, Mr. Speaker, what we have seen in this house tonight is a repetition in kind of that sorry spectacle.
You will remember that amazing episode, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition- and those of us who have known him a long time were hoping for something better on that occasion, in fact, something a whole lot
IMr. Pearson.]
better from him, and then to everybody's chagrin-and I am sure most of all to the chagrin of his friends and followers-what was brought in, that monumental amendment to a supply motion just like today, Mr. Speaker, in which he asked that:
His Excellency's advisers should, In the opinion of this house, submit their resignation forthwith.
Mr. Speaker, he made constitutional history that day and it was not very good constitutional history, either, and what he has done today is not very much better. We have heard from the hon. gentleman this night statements that would, if taken seriously by anyone in this house,-and I am sure they will not be-condemn this government fore and aft, foot, horse and artillery, everything, and yet, Mr. Speaker, does he say that His Excellency's advisers should submit their resignations as being unfit to hold office? No. That one apparently is taboo now. That one is not to be repeated since the 20th day of January. The effects that time were not of a kind to be desired ever again by the hon. gentleman. One would have thought that there might at least have been room in the amendment for some denunciation of His Excellency's advisers after the cascades and torrents of, I shall not say abuse but at least of invective, invective hurled at the head of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), hurled at the government. Mr. Speaker, it was a great opportunity for the hon. gentleman to match his brave words and his accusations with something at least manly and courageous in the amendment. But what do our disappointed eyes behold? This is the squib:
This house is of the opinion that the actions of the government in connection with "The Canadian Economic Outlook"-
This is in quotations, Mr. Speaker; there is no date given to it. I continue:
-have seriously weakened the value of confidential advice from civil servants with resultant damage to the proper formulation of economic and fiscal policies.

Let us deal with the issues that have been raised here, Mr. Speaker. We are told, for instance, that we did not give the people of Canada sufficient pessimism in the budget forecast. Here is the story, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen can judge now, in the light of the assumptions that were referred by the Leader of the Opposition tonight, whether this budget forecast was based upon a sound estimate of all the factors at work in the Canadian economy on June 17 when the budget was delivered in the house. For instance, as found at page 1231 of Hansard, I began with this reference in the four pages of review of the economic situation to be found at pages 1231 to 1235. I began, Mr. Speaker, with this statement;
During the past eighteen months Canada shared with most of the rest of the world some slackening in the pace of economic growth. Business activity declined in the United States, and the rate of expansion slowed in western Europe. In Canada unemployment emerged as a serious problem and declining business capital investment as a significant developing tendency. Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to forget that there were solid achievements on the economic side and developments which augur well for the future.
Will anyone say that is an unbalanced statement or that the government turned its back upon the less favourable features in the economic situation as of that time? Then further along on the page I refer to the fact that the rate of economic growth slowed noticeably during 1957. Then as found at page 1232, I said:
The most important change which emerged during 1957 was the decline in the importance of business capital investment as a dynamic force in our economy, particularly investment in our resource industries.
Yet the Leader of the Opposition tonight has the temerity to say that the Minister of Finance in his budget speech did not take account of the decline in the amount of business capital investment in the economic life of this country. It is unfortunate that the hon. gentleman did not read the speech but contented himself with reading some excerpts from my speech that were quoted in the Toronto Star. If he is talking about excerpts, why does he not read the full document that was open to him to read? He has given an example here of a man who is very selective about excerpts when they serve his purpose. Again, Mr. Speaker, as found at page 1232 of Hansard, I said:
Early in 1957 many commodity markets moved into a position of over-supply.
And again:
By mid-1957 the value of large capital projects being started began to run behind the value of projects being completed.

Then again I make this reference:
In 1956 capital expenditure rose by 20 per cent and together with increased inventory accumulation accounted for almost one-half the very large increase in total demand. In 1957 there was a much more moderate rise of nine per cent in capital expenditure. More important was the fact that during 1956 capital expenditure was rising at a rapid rate while in 1957 investment outlays as a whole first levelled out and then declined slightly. The slow-down in the rate of capital investment was accentuated by the inventory liquidation which developed toward the end of the year. This reduction in inventories continued into the first quarter of 1958, which has meant that to some extent the demands for goods is being met out of stocks rather than giving rise to new production.
And again:
Although business capital investment ended the year on a weaker note than it had begun,-
And again:
Consumer expenditure was an important sustaining force in 1957, and at the end of 1957 was running about four per cent higher than a year earlier. Expenditure on durable goods, however, showed practically no increase over the previous year, reflecting in part the slower growth of incomes but also the rapid expansion in 1955 and 1956 which was based upon large increases in consumer credit.
And again, Mr. Speaker, at page 1233 we find the following:
The combination of somewhat less favourable employment opportunities with a rapidly expanding labour force resulted in an increase in unemployment. As employment was higher through 1957 than through 1956, so also was unemployment.
For 1957 as a whole the average number of persons without jobs and seeking work was 254,000, an increase of 75,000 over 1956. As a percentage of the labour force, unemployment in 1957 averaged 4.3 per cent, equalling the rate in 1954.
Again in the second column on page 1233 I said:
Corporate profits declined by 11 per cent as costs rose and markets became more competitive.
And again:
Personal saving was down about 5 per cent-
Does this suggest that in this budget presentation we ignored the less agreeable facts of the situation? Does this suggest any attempt to gloss over the unfavourable factors? Leader of the Opposition was tonight trying to persuade the house to believe it was but, of course, he was selective. He was not looking for any opportunity to give a balanced presentation-

Business of the House 4 on today's order paper, the act respecting the taxation of estates; then item No. 13, the Loan Companies Act which is to be referred to the banking and commerce committee; and then item No. 14, an act to amend the Trust Companies Act which is also to be referred to the banking and commerce committee; and then the resolution concerning the Customs Tariff amendments.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What numbers, please?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is item No. 22. And then we will take item No. 6, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act; item No. 15, second reading

of the act to amend the Financial Administration Act; and item No. 11, second reading of an act to amend the Income Tax Act. We hope to finish all of this tomorrow.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What does the house leader intend to do on Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On Wednesday we have to ask for interim supply and then we would take any of these measures I have mentioned which had not previously been dealt with.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Tuesday, August 5, 1958
